As the Earth orbits around the Sun, the tilt means that at different times of the year, the Sun is shining directly on the Earth's equator, and at other times, it is shining at higher or lower angles in relation to the equator.

During winter, the Earth's axial tilt means that the Sun's rays are hitting the Earth at a more oblique angle, causing the Sun to appear lower in the sky and resulting in shorter days and less sunlight. During summer, the opposite is true: the Sun's rays hit the Earth at a more direct angle, leading to longer days and more sunlight.

This is why the Earth's axial tilt causes the cycle of the seasons, including changes in the amount of daylight during different times of the year.
